title: The Burnt Raisin
part: PART ONE: THE SHOP AT THE END OF INK LANE

pages.text:
*The First Rule of Mapmaking: A map is a promise.*

Nobody in the city of Verrin was awake yet, except the gulls, the baker, and Tam Marrow, who was grinding ink and hating it.

There is a way of grinding oak-gall ink that Master Finch called "listening," and a way that Tam called "trying not to throw the pestle at the wall." It involved a stone bowl, a lump of something that looked like a burnt raisin, and a great deal of patience, and Tam had exactly as much patience as an eleven-year-old has at half past five in the morning, which is to say, none. She ground. The raisin crumbled. Grey powder puffed up her nose, and she sneezed a black freckle onto her wrist to keep the other freckles company.

Outside the shop window the sky was the color of weak tea. Somewhere below, the river Aln was muttering under all its bridges. Tam scowled at the pestle, and the pestle, being a pestle, said nothing.
pages.image: Tam, a sturdy 11-year-old girl with a black braid tied with blue string and ink-stained fingers, scowls as she grinds ink in a stone bowl in a dim old map shop at dawn, powder dusting her nose; a window showing a pale sky behind her.

pages.text:
The stairs at the back of the shop creaked in three places, which was how Tam always knew Master Finch was coming, and also how Master Finch always knew Tam was pretending not to have been sulking.

Odalys Finch came down them one step at a time, tall and thin as a heron, with her white hair in a bun stuck all over with pencils and her lavender scarf trailing behind her like a slow purple comet. She tapped her hawthorn cane on the last stair, peered over her round spectacles, and dipped one trembling finger into the bowl.

"Better," she said.

"It's terrible," said Tam.

"It is better than yesterday's, which was better than the day before's. That is how one arrives at a good ink." She wiped her finger on her scarf, which explained the scarf. "Do go on grinding. I shall stand here being encouraging."

The shop around them was crowded with maps: maps rolled in racks like sleeping cats, maps pinned to the beams, maps of coasts and moors and mountain passes, and one very large brass globe with a dent in the north where somebody had once dropped a cheese.
pages.image: Master Finch, a tall thin old woman with white hair in a bun full of pencils, round spectacles and a lavender scarf, leans on a hawthorn cane and dips a finger in Tam's ink bowl; behind them racks of rolled maps and a dented brass globe in a cluttered shop.

pages.text:
Now, you should know where Tam came from, because Tam never stopped knowing it.

She came from the Lowtide Docks, where the mud was deep and the gulls were rude and nobody's mother ever seemed to be at home. She had sorted fish before she could properly count them. She had run errands for six different net-menders and tied forty kinds of knot by the age of seven. She had learned her letters at nine, from a one-eyed man who mended nets and read the shipping notices aloud in a voice like a rusty hinge, and she had learned them fast, because she had been terrified of being the last person on the docks who couldn't.

Then one grey morning she had repaired a cracked compass for a stranger, using a fish-hook and a bit of wax, and the stranger had turned out to be Master Finch.

"I don't need an apprentice with clever hands," Finch had told her afterward. "I need one who doesn't say 'it can't be done.' You said it four times and then you did it anyway. That will do."
pages.image: A younger-looking scene in the dockside: Tam kneels on a muddy wooden dock among fish crates and nets, carefully mending a small cracked brass compass with a fish-hook, while a tall old woman in a lavender scarf watches with interest; gulls circle overhead.

pages.text:
On the table by the window lay the small stitched notebook that Finch called the Yesterday Book.

Every evening before supper, Tam drew exactly one thing in it: a river, a wobbling stripe of ink with two bends in the middle, the same river every night. Beneath it she wrote one honest sentence. *Straighter at the top. Blot at the corner.* *Too fast. Ugly.* That was the whole exercise, and Tam thought it was the most boring thing in the kingdom of Aldermere, and she had done it for seven months.

Finch turned the pages now, slowly, with her shaky fingers. The rivers went by, page after page, each one a whisker straighter than the one before it, like a person very slowly learning to walk.

Tam saw only how crooked the last one still was. She said, to the ceiling, "The Academy children could draw that in their sleep."

Finch didn't answer. She merely closed the book with great gentleness, the way you close a door on a room where something is growing.
pages.image: Master Finch turns the pages of a small stitched notebook full of wobbly hand-drawn rivers, while Tam stands beside her arms crossed, looking at the ceiling; a sunbeam falls across a slanted drawing table.

pages.text:
A bell began to ring in the street outside, a big flat brass handbell, clanging over the sound of the gulls, and a voice came rolling down Ink Lane like a barrel down a hill.

Tam went to the window with the pestle still in her fist. Below, the town crier was planting himself in front of the shop in his red coat and feathered hat, puffing out his chest.

"By order of the Mapmakers' Guild of Verrin," he bellowed, "hear ye, hear ye! The Grand Survey of the Uncharted Marches is proclaimed!"

Behind her a pencil hit the floor. Tam turned. Master Finch was standing very still with her hand at her collar, and on her long, lined face was a smile Tam had never seen before: the smile of a person who has been waiting a very, very long time for a particular door to open.
pages.image: Tam at a shop window looking down at a town crier in a red coat and feathered hat ringing a brass handbell in a narrow cobbled lane, while behind her Master Finch stands still with a pencil fallen at her feet and an astonished smile.
